questions.title: Docker Containers vs Virtual Machines
questions.question: What is Docker and how do containers differ from virtual machines?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Container: process isolation using Linux namespaces and cgroups — shares host kernel
- VM: full OS virtualization — hypervisor emulates hardware, each VM has own kernel
- Container advantages: milliseconds to start, MB in size, low overhead
- VM advantages: stronger isolation, different OS/kernel, better security boundaries
- Docker image: read-only filesystem layers; container: running image instance + writable layer
- Docker Hub / ECR: container registries for storing and distributing images
- Use case: containers for application packaging and deployment; VMs for strong isolation

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Docker containers are process isolation mechanisms — they use Linux kernel features like namespaces and control groups to make a process think it has its own filesystem, network, and process space, while actually sharing the host kernel. Virtual machines emulate entire hardware and run a completely separate kernel. This makes containers dramatically more lightweight: a container starts in milliseconds and uses megabytes, while a VM takes minutes to boot and uses gigabytes.

The tradeoff is isolation strength. Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability could theoretically affect all containers on that host. VMs have a hypervisor boundary that provides much stronger isolation. For most web application workloads, container isolation is sufficient. For multi-tenant environments where you're running code from different customers, VMs or stronger container isolation techniques are used.

A Docker image is a stack of read-only filesystem layers built from a Dockerfile. Each instruction creates a new layer. When you run an image as a container, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top. Multiple containers can run from the same image without duplicating the read-only data — they all share the image layers.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Container vs VM Architecture

```
Virtual Machines:
┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
│  App + Libs  │  │  App + Libs  │
│  Guest OS    │  │  Guest OS    │  (each has full OS — 2-20GB each)
└──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘
       └────────┬─────────┘
          Hypervisor
          Host OS
          Hardware

Docker Containers:
┌────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐
│App+Libs│  │App+Libs│  │App+Libs│  (just app + deps — 50-500MB each)
└────┬───┘  └────┬───┘  └────┬───┘
     └───────────┼────────────┘
             Docker Engine
             Host OS Kernel (shared)
             Hardware
```

## Image Layers

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre        # Layer 1: base JRE (~200MB, pulled once)
WORKDIR /app                        # Layer 2: create directory
COPY target/app.jar .               # Layer 3: your JAR (~50MB)
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# Layer 1 is cached and reused across all your Spring Boot images
# Only layer 3 changes on each build → fast rebuilds
```

## Essential Docker Commands

```bash
# Build image
docker build -t my-app:1.0 .
docker build -t my-app:1.0 --no-cache .  # rebuild from scratch

# Run container
docker run -d --name my-app \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e DB_HOST=postgres \
  --network my-network \
  my-app:1.0

# Inspect and debug
docker logs my-app -f          # stream logs
docker exec -it my-app /bin/sh  # interactive shell
docker stats my-app             # CPU/memory usage

# Cleanup
docker stop my-app && docker rm my-app
docker image prune -f           # remove unused images
```

speakable_v2.hook: Docker containers are process isolation mechanisms — they use Linux kernel features like namespaces and control groups to make a process think it has its own filesystem, network, and process space, while actually sharing the.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Multiple containers can run from the same image without duplicating the read-only data — they all share the image layers.

questions.title: Writing Optimal Dockerfiles for Java
questions.question: How do you write an optimal Dockerfile for a Spring Boot Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Multi-stage build: builder stage with JDK, final stage with lean JRE
- Layer caching: COPY dependencies before source code — rebuild only changed layers
- Spring Boot layered JAR: explode JAR layers for optimal caching (dependencies rarely change)
- Non-root user: run container as non-root for security
- .dockerignore: exclude target/, .git/, test files from build context
- JVM flags for containers: -XX:+UseContainerSupport, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
- Healthcheck in Dockerfile or Docker Compose for container health monitoring

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The two key optimizations for Spring Boot Dockerfiles are multi-stage builds and layered JAR extraction. Multi-stage builds use a full JDK image to compile and package, then copy only the output into a lean JRE image. This makes the final image 3-5 times smaller — no compiler, no Maven, no test dependencies.

Layered JAR extraction takes advantage of Spring Boot's ability to split the JAR into layers based on how frequently they change: snapshot dependencies at the bottom, regular dependencies, Spring Boot loader, application classes at the top. The lower layers rarely change, so Docker caches them. When you push a new version, only the application layer needs to be transferred. This dramatically speeds up deployments in CI/CD.

Always run your container as a non-root user. If a process inside a container is compromised, a non-root user limits the blast radius. Create a dedicated application user in the Dockerfile and switch to it before the ENTRYPOINT.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Optimal Spring Boot Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# ===== Stage 1: Build =====
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /build

# Cache Maven dependencies separately (only re-runs if pom.xml changes)
COPY pom.xml .
COPY .mvn .mvn
COPY mvnw .
RUN ./mvnw dependency:go-offline -q

# Build app
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests -q

# Extract layered JAR for optimal caching
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/*.jar extract --destination /layers

# ===== Stage 2: Runtime =====
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app

# Security: non-root user
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

# Copy layers from least-changed to most-changed (Docker caches lower layers)
COPY --from=builder --chown=appuser:appgroup /layers/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=appuser:appgroup /layers/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=appuser:appgroup /layers/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=appuser:appgroup /layers/application/ ./

USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080

# Container-aware JVM settings
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:+UseContainerSupport \
               -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
               -XX:+UseG1GC \
               -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom"

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=60s --retries=3 \
    CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1

ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```

## .dockerignore

```
# .dockerignore — exclude from build context
target/
.git/
.gitignore
*.md
DOCKERFILE
docker-compose*.yml
.idea/
*.iml
test-results/
```

## Image Size Comparison

```
Without multi-stage (JDK + fat JAR):  ~500MB
With multi-stage (JRE + fat JAR):     ~250MB
With multi-stage + layered JAR:       ~250MB but deploys MUCH faster
→ Only the application layer (~5MB) transferred on code changes
```

speakable_v2.hook: The two key optimizations for Spring Boot Dockerfiles are multi-stage builds and layered JAR extraction.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Create a dedicated application user in the Dockerfile and switch to it before the ENTRYPOINT.

questions.title: Docker Volumes and Networking
questions.question: How do Docker volumes and networking work, and how do containers communicate with each other?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Volume: persists data outside container lifecycle — survives container restarts and removals
- Named volume: managed by Docker, best for databases and persistent data
- Bind mount: mounts host directory — useful for dev hot-reload but not for production
- Networks: bridge (default), host, none
- User-defined bridge network: containers can communicate by container name (DNS resolution)
- Default bridge: containers use IP, no DNS — less useful
- Port mapping: -p hostPort:containerPort
- Container DNS: on user-defined network, container name = hostname

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Docker volumes decouple data from the container lifecycle. A container is ephemeral — when you stop and remove it, the writable layer is gone. Volumes persist data independently, so your database data survives container restarts, updates, and replacements. Named volumes are managed by Docker — you don't need to know where on the host the data is stored.

For container communication, use user-defined bridge networks rather than the default bridge. On a user-defined network, Docker provides automatic DNS resolution — containers can reach each other by their service or container name. If your Spring Boot app and PostgreSQL container are both on the same network, the app can connect to postgres:5432 where postgres is the PostgreSQL container name.

Bind mounts are useful in development — you mount your source code directory into the container and the application sees live changes without rebuilding the image. In production, always use named volumes for persistent data and never bind-mount your entire source tree.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Volumes

```bash
# Named volume — Docker manages location
docker volume create postgres-data

docker run -d \
  --name postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16-alpine

# Bind mount — mount host directory (dev only)
docker run -d \
  --name spring-dev \
  -v $(pwd)/src:/app/src \
  -v $(pwd)/target:/app/target \
  my-app:dev
```

## Networks

```bash
# Create a user-defined network
docker network create app-network

# Run PostgreSQL on the network
docker run -d \
  --name postgres \
  --network app-network \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=appdb \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  postgres:16-alpine

# Run Spring Boot on same network
docker run -d \
  --name spring-api \
  --network app-network \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/appdb \
  #                                                ↑ container name = hostname
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret \
  my-app:latest

# spring-api can reach postgres by hostname 'postgres'
# No IP addresses needed — Docker DNS handles it
```

## Inspect Container Network

```bash
docker network inspect app-network
# Shows all containers on the network and their IPs

docker exec spring-api ping postgres  # verify connectivity by name
docker exec spring-api wget -qO- http://redis:6379  # test another service
```

speakable_v2.hook: Docker volumes decouple data from the container lifecycle.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: In production, always use named volumes for persistent data and never bind-mount your entire source tree.

questions.title: Docker Security Best Practices
questions.question: What are the key security best practices for running Docker containers in production?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Run as non-root user — always specify USER in Dockerfile
- Read-only filesystem: --read-only flag, tmpfs for temp files
- No sensitive data in image: use runtime env vars or secrets mounts
- Scan images for vulnerabilities: docker scout, trivy, snyk
- Minimal base image: distroless or alpine to reduce attack surface
- Drop capabilities: --cap-drop=ALL, add only needed capabilities
- Secrets: use Docker secrets or secret mounts — not environment variables for sensitive data
- Resource limits: --memory and --cpus prevent resource exhaustion

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The most impactful security improvements for containers are running as a non-root user and using minimal base images. If a container runs as root and an attacker exploits a vulnerability in your application, they have root access inside the container, which can be leveraged to escape to the host. Running as a non-root user dramatically limits what an attacker can do.

Minimal base images reduce the attack surface. Every tool in the image is a potential vector. Alpine-based images have only essential utilities. Distroless images go further — they contain only the runtime and your application, no shell, no package manager. If there's no bash in the container, an attacker who gets code execution can't easily move around.

Never put secrets in Dockerfile or image layers. Docker image history shows every layer, and committing a secret makes it visible to anyone who can pull the image. Use environment variables at runtime for non-sensitive configuration, and Docker secrets or secret mounts for sensitive values.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Secure Dockerfile Practices

```dockerfile
# Use specific version — not 'latest' (reproducible builds)
FROM eclipse-temurin:21.0.3_9-jre-alpine

# Create non-root user before COPY
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

WORKDIR /app
RUN chown appuser:appgroup /app

COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup target/app.jar .

# Switch to non-root BEFORE ENTRYPOINT
USER appuser

# Don't expose ports >= 1024 to avoid privilege issues
EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# NEVER:
# ENV DB_PASSWORD=mysecret  ← visible in docker history
# COPY .env .  ← don't copy secrets into image
```

## Runtime Security Flags

```bash
# Minimal capabilities, read-only filesystem, resource limits
docker run -d \
  --name spring-api \
  --user 1001:1001 \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=100m,mode=1777 \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --memory=512m \
  --cpus=1.0 \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  my-app:latest
```

## Vulnerability Scanning

```bash
# Trivy — free, fast, comprehensive
trivy image my-app:latest

# Docker Scout (built into Docker)
docker scout cves my-app:latest

# GitHub Actions: scan before push
- name: Scan for vulnerabilities
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: my-app:${{ github.sha }}
    severity: 'HIGH,CRITICAL'
    exit-code: '1'  # fail build if critical vulnerabilities found
```

## Environment Variables vs Secrets

```bash
# OK for non-sensitive config
docker run -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod ...

# Sensitive data: use --secret or inject at runtime from Secrets Manager
docker run --secret id=db_password,env=DB_PASSWORD ...
# or: read from AWS Secrets Manager at startup (recommended)
```

speakable_v2.hook: The most impactful security improvements for containers are running as a non-root user and using minimal base images.
speakable_v2.cap: Use environment variables at runtime for non-sensitive configuration, and Docker secrets or secret mounts for sensitive values.

questions.title: Docker Resource Limits and JVM Tuning
questions.question: How do you set resource limits for Docker containers running Java/Spring Boot applications?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- --memory: hard container memory limit — OOMKilled if exceeded
- --cpus: fractional CPU limit — 0.5 = half a core
- JVM in containers: before Java 11 didn't respect container limits — used host RAM
- -XX:+UseContainerSupport (default Java 11+): JVM reads cgroup limits from container
- -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0: JVM uses 75% of container memory for heap
- Metaspace: off-heap — doesn't count toward heap but counts toward container memory limit
- OOM: application OOM vs container OOM — understand difference
- G1GC (default Java 9+): good for containers; ZGC for low-latency

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Before Java 11, the JVM didn't understand it was running in a container. It read available RAM from the host OS and sized the heap accordingly — a 512MB container running on a 32GB host would try to use 8GB for the heap, immediately causing the container to be killed for exceeding its memory limit.

From Java 11 onwards, UseContainerSupport is enabled by default. The JVM reads its cgroup memory limit — the container's actual limit — and sizes the heap as a percentage of that. With -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0, a 1GB container gets 768MB for the Java heap, leaving 256MB for off-heap memory: Metaspace, thread stacks, native memory, and OS overhead.

The right pattern is to set the container memory limit, let the JVM auto-size its heap from that limit using MaxRAMPercentage, and monitor both JVM heap usage and total container RSS. If the container is being OOMKilled, either the heap limit is too high for non-heap needs, or the application has a memory leak.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Dockerfile JVM Configuration

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/app.jar app.jar

# UseContainerSupport is default in Java 11+
# MaxRAMPercentage: heap = 75% of container memory limit
# MaxMetaspaceSize: cap off-heap class metadata
ENV JAVA_OPTS="\
  -XX:+UseContainerSupport \
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
  -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heap-dump.hprof \
  -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom"

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]
```

## docker run / Compose Resource Limits

```bash
# docker run
docker run \
  --memory=1g \
  --memory-swap=1g \
  --cpus=0.5 \
  my-spring-app
# --memory: 1GB RAM limit
# --memory-swap = --memory: no swap (swap = 0)
# --cpus=0.5: 50% of one CPU
```

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    image: my-spring-app
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 1G
          cpus: '0.5'
        reservations:
          memory: 512M
          cpus: '0.25'
```

## Memory Budget Calculation

```
Container memory limit: 1024 MB

JVM Heap (MaxRAMPercentage=75%)  =  768 MB
Metaspace (MaxMetaspaceSize)     =  256 MB
Thread stacks (200 threads×1MB)  =  200 MB
CodeCache                        =   64 MB
OS/libc overhead                 =   64 MB
                                 ----------
Total needed                     = 1352 MB  ← EXCEEDS 1024MB!

Fix: increase container to 1.5GB, or
     reduce MaxRAMPercentage to 60%:
     768MB × 0.6 = 460MB heap
     460 + 256 + 200 + 64 + 64 = 1044MB ≈ fits in 1GB
```

speakable_v2.hook: Before Java 11, the JVM didn't understand it was running in a container.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: If the container is being OOMKilled, either the heap limit is too high for non-heap needs, or the application has a memory leak.

questions.title: Multi-Stage Docker Builds for Java
questions.question: How do you optimize Docker image size and build speed for Spring Boot applications using multi-stage builds?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Multi-stage build: separate build environment from runtime image — smaller, more secure final image
- JDK in build stage, JRE in runtime stage — JDK ~500MB → JRE ~200MB → JRE Alpine ~85MB
- Layer caching: COPY pom.xml + RUN mvn dependency:go-offline BEFORE COPY src — cache deps layer
- Spring Boot layered JAR: extract layers for better cache reuse
- .dockerignore: exclude target/, .git/, *.md — faster context transfer
- BuildKit: parallel stage building, improved cache
- Distroless images: minimal attack surface — no shell, no package manager

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Multi-stage builds are essential for Java because the build environment needs the full JDK and Maven or Gradle, but the runtime environment only needs the JRE to execute the compiled JAR. The final image has no source code, no build tools, no Maven cache — only the minimal runtime and the application JAR.

Layer caching is the key to fast builds in CI. Docker caches each layer and only rebuilds from the point where something changed. The critical optimization is separating dependency download from source compilation. Copy pom.xml and run mvn dependency:go-offline before copying source code. Dependencies change rarely; source code changes every commit. This way, dependency download is cached and skipped unless pom.xml changes.

Spring Boot 2.3+ introduced layered JARs. Instead of one fat JAR, the application is split into layers by how often they change: dependencies (rarely), Spring Boot itself (occasionally), your application code (frequently). Each layer becomes a Docker layer, maximizing cache reuse when only code changes.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Optimized Multi-Stage Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: Build — uses full JDK + Maven
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Copy ONLY dependency files first — cache this layer
COPY pom.xml .
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY mvnw .
RUN chmod +x mvnw && ./mvnw dependency:go-offline -q
# ^ This layer is cached unless pom.xml changes

# Now copy source — this invalidates cache only when code changes
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests -q

# Extract Spring Boot layers
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/*.jar extract

# Stage 2: Runtime — uses minimal JRE
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app

# Non-root user for security
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

# Copy Spring Boot layers in order (slowest to fastest changing)
# Each COPY = Docker layer = individual caching
COPY --from=builder /app/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/application/ ./

ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:+UseContainerSupport -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0"
EXPOSE 8080

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=60s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1

ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher"]
```

## .dockerignore

```
target/
.git/
.gitignore
*.md
.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.jar
docker-compose*.yml
**/*.log
.env
```

## Image Size Comparison

```
No optimization (fat JAR on JDK image):   ~600 MB
Multi-stage, JRE Alpine, no layers:       ~200 MB
Multi-stage, JRE Alpine, Spring layers:   ~200 MB (but better layer cache)
Distroless JRE:                           ~130 MB

Spring Boot layered build cache hit:
  Without layers: rebuild + push ~120MB JAR every commit
  With layers: only app layer (~5MB) pushed when only code changes
```

speakable_v2.hook: Multi-stage builds are essential for Java because the build environment needs the full JDK and Maven or Gradle, but the runtime environment only needs the JRE to execute the compiled JAR.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Each layer becomes a Docker layer, maximizing cache reuse when only code changes.
